agree.reason: The parallel between a lab and a plant is believable, but a skeptical HR manager gets a letter addressed to '[Hiring Manager's Name]' at '[Company]' with an unfinished AP sentence, and it gives her no proof on records, which is her main doubt, so a phone screen is uncertain.

honest.reason: It rightly drops the unsupported claim about halving training time, but it understates the GMP course as something she 'plans to start' when she is already enrolled and finishes May 2, and the 90-day plan promises more than the facts show.

works_the_facts.reason: It leaves out the strongest figure, that she cut new-teacher training from 20 hours to 12 (40%), and it doesn't state the AP gain as 17 points or a roughly 41% relative rise, or the total of about 18 teachers trained.

right_comparison.reason: The AP pass rate is shown as a trend from 41% to 58%, but the training-time claim has no 20-hour baseline, so the reader has nothing real to compare 'shortening onboarding' against.

qualification.reason: The 90-day promise of 'a target you can hold me to' names no number, and the GMP course has no completion date, so the reader cannot check either one.

objections.reason: It raises the GMP-records gap itself but leaves out the signed training records she keeps and the two clean state audits, which largely answer that objection, and it never gives her June 14 start date or interview availability.

fit.reason: It is a one-page cover letter as asked, but the bracketed placeholders remain for her name, the company and the HR manager, even though she knows all three.
